items.subtitle: What is Node2D?
items.contents:
What is Node2D?

Node2D is a 2D game engine and visual editor for making games for the web. You build a game by creating Scenes, placing Nodes, adding Components, creating visual scripts with ScriptNodes, importing assets, and testing with Play or Debug.

You can save projects, export them as a project file, and export a playable web package. The editor can also work as an installable/offline-capable web app.

items.subtitle: How the editor works
items.contents:
How the editor works

The main parts you work with are the Scene tree, viewport, Node Components, ScriptNode editor, Asset Manager, Camera, Game Settings, and project controls.

  1. Create or load a project.
  2. Create a Scene.
  3. Add Nodes.
  4. Add Components to make Nodes visible, physical, or interactive.
  5. Build ScriptNode logic.
  6. Add assets such as images and audio.
  7. Test with Play or Debug.
  8. Save or export the project.

items.subtitle: Important editor idea
items.contents:
Project → Scene → Node

A Project contains your game. A Scene is one game screen, level, menu, or area. A Node is an object inside a Scene. Components give a Node features, and ScriptNodes give it visual logic.

items.subtitle: Viewport navigation
items.contents:
Viewport navigation

Use the viewport to look around your Scene. You can pan, zoom, center the view, and use Select, Move, Rotate, Scale, or All tools to edit Nodes.

When a new ScriptNode is placed, it is placed around the part of the ScriptNode workspace you are currently looking at, so you do not have to search for it elsewhere.

items.subtitle: Small screen warning
items.contents:
Small screen warning

When the editor is too narrow for comfortable editing, it shows a full-screen warning and temporarily blocks editing. Widen the window or rotate your device to continue.

items.subtitle: Build a game from start to finish
items.contents:
Build a game from start to finish

A practical Node2D workflow is to build one small playable idea first, then grow it. Start with a Scene, add a player Node, give it a Sprite and Collider, then add the Nodes it needs to interact with.

  1. Create a project. Give the project a name you can recognize later.
  2. Set up the starting Scene. Add or rename the first Scene and choose it as the Preferred Scene in Game Settings.
  3. Create the player. Add a Node, choose a Sprite asset for it, and position it in the Scene.
  4. Add game objects. Create ground, enemies, collectibles, buttons, UI elements, or other Nodes.
  5. Add Components. Use Collider for collision shapes, Physics for physical motion, Text for labels, Progress Bar for meters, and Joystick for touch controls.
  6. Add behavior. Open the Node's Script and connect an Event to the Actions and Controls that should happen.
  7. Test early. Press Play often. It is easier to find a wrong position, collision, input, or script connection before the Scene becomes large.
  8. Save and export. Save the project so it can be restored, then use Export Project when you have a playable web build.

You can build a simple game without putting every object into one giant script. Keep each Node responsible for the behavior that belongs to that object.

items.subtitle: Top bar
items.contents:
Top bar

The top bar contains the main project, editing, view, help, and runtime controls. As the window becomes narrower, labels can hide so the controls remain usable.

At very small widths, the editing mode controls move into a vertical group on the right side instead of overlapping other controls.

items.subtitle: Select, Move, Rotate, Scale, All
items.contents:
Editing tools

ToolWhat it does
SelectSelect Nodes or objects.
MoveMove selected objects.
RotateRotate selected objects.
ScaleResize selected objects.
AllUse the combined editing mode.

items.subtitle: Multi-selection
items.contents:
Multi-selection

Selection behaves like common desktop file selection.

  • Click an item to select it.
  • Ctrl-click (or Cmd-click on supported systems) adds or removes one item from the selection.
  • Shift-click selects a range from the current selection anchor.
  • Operations such as copy, cut, duplicate, move, and delete can apply to the selected group when supported.

This works for supported editor lists and object selections instead of requiring a special selection system for every item.

items.subtitle: Context menus
items.contents:
Context menus

Right-click or use the available context-menu shortcut to open actions for the selected item. Context menus are limited to the available screen area so their list can scroll instead of extending beyond the screen.

items.subtitle: Help
items.contents:
Help

The ? Help button opens the help page inside the editor in a modal window. Close the modal when you are finished.

items.subtitle: Fullscreen
items.contents:
Fullscreen

The Fullscreen button expands the editor to fullscreen. The icon and its button area are one clickable control, so clicking the icon or the surrounding button activates fullscreen.

items.subtitle: Keyboard shortcut editing
items.contents:
Keyboard shortcut editing

Editor shortcuts can be changed in Editor Settings. Your chosen shortcuts are saved locally on your device and are used again when you reopen the editor.

items.subtitle: Snapping
items.contents:
Snapping

Snapping makes editing use fixed intervals instead of letting values land at arbitrary decimal positions or scales. It is useful when you want objects to line up on a predictable grid or you want repeated size changes to be consistent.

Move / Scale Snap controls the interval used by Node movement and scaling. For example, a value of 0.1 means a position or scale value is rounded to steps such as 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, and so on.

Rotate Snap controls the angle interval. 0° turns rotation snapping off; a value such as 90° makes rotations land at 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°, and so on.

Snapping applies while dragging the Move, Scale, and Rotate gizmos, including their center/axis controls. It is an editing aid, not a physics rule: it changes the values you create in the editor.

items.subtitle: Scale gizmo
items.contents:
Scale gizmo

The Scale gizmo appears around the selected Node when Scale or All mode is active. Its small boxes are resize handles.

  • Corner handles resize in both directions while preserving the object's starting width-to-height ratio.
  • Left / right handles resize horizontally.
  • Top / bottom handles resize vertically.

When a scale handle is being dragged, the active handle is given an additional outline so you can see exactly which resize point is being used.

The scale operation still follows your Move / Scale Snap setting. A snap value of 0.1 prevents tiny floating-point changes from producing values such as 1.0000000001 during normal gizmo editing.

items.subtitle: Reload and close protection
items.contents:
Reload and close protection

When a project is loaded, Node2D can prevent an accidental browser refresh or tab close from happening silently. The browser may show its standard confirmation dialog so you have a chance to stay on the page.

This browser protection does not replace saving. Use Save or Auto Save so your work is actually stored before leaving.

items.subtitle: Gizmo size while zooming
items.contents:
Gizmo size while zooming

The Move, Rotate, and Scale editing controls stay visually usable while you zoom the viewport. Their handles use screen-aware sizing instead of becoming tiny or huge only because the Node itself is large or small on the screen.

The object outline still represents the actual object size, while the editing handles remain easy to grab.

items.subtitle: Move gizmo
items.contents:
Move gizmo

The Move gizmo has a center control and directional arrows. Drag the center to move freely. Drag the horizontal arrow to move horizontally, and drag the vertical arrow to move vertically.

Move Snap from Editor Settings determines the fixed editing interval used while moving. A value of 1 means movement is snapped to whole units.

items.subtitle: What is a Scene?
items.contents:
What is a Scene?

A Scene is a collection of Nodes and folders. Use different Scenes for levels, menus, rooms, screens, or other parts of a game.

items.subtitle: Create and rename Scenes
items.contents:
Create and rename Scenes

Use + Add Scene to create another Scene. Select a Scene to work on it, and use the available rename action to change its name.

items.subtitle: Preferred Scene
items.contents:
Preferred Scene

The Preferred Scene in Game Settings is the Scene that starts when you press Play or Debug.

items.subtitle: Scene list and menu size
items.contents:
Scene list

The Scene list and Scene drop-down/context menu stay within the available screen height. When there are many Scenes, the list becomes scrollable. The + Add Scene control stays outside the scrollable part so it remains easy to reach.

items.subtitle: Folders
items.contents:
Folders

Folders help organize Nodes inside a Scene. They do not act as game objects themselves. You can expand and collapse them to keep the Scene tree manageable.

items.subtitle: Moving Nodes
items.contents:
Moving Nodes

Nodes can be moved between folders or back to the Scene root using the available tree controls or drag-and-drop where supported.

items.subtitle: What is a Node?
items.contents:
What is a Node?

A Node is an object placed in a Scene. A Node can represent a player, enemy, item, button, decoration, platform, effect, or another game object.

Nodes have a name and ID and can contain Components and a visual ScriptNode graph.

items.subtitle: Node name and ID
items.contents:
Node name and ID

The name is the label you see in the Scene tree and selectors. The numeric ID helps identify the Node when it is referenced by editor and game systems.

items.subtitle: Node selection
items.contents:
Node selection

Select Nodes from the Scene tree or viewport. A selected Node shows its available Components and can be edited with the viewport tools.

items.subtitle: Node copy, paste, and duplicate
items.contents:
Copy, paste, and duplicate

Copy and paste or Duplicate can create another Node with its Components and ScriptNode setup. Multiple selected Nodes can be handled together where the editor supports the operation.

items.subtitle: Deleting Nodes
items.contents:
Deleting Nodes

Delete or Backspace removes selected editor objects after the editor's confirmation rules are applied.

items.subtitle: Node
items.contents:
Node Component

The Node component represents the Node itself.

PropertyMeaning
NameName shown in the Scene tree and selectors.
IDNumeric identifier for the Node.

This component is built into every Node.

items.subtitle: Script
items.contents:
Script Component

The Script component contains the Node's visual ScriptNode graph. Open it to build the Node's behavior.

The graph belongs to that Node, so each Node has its own ScriptNode workspace.

References: Follow Object · Create Object · Chase · Avoid · Expressions

items.subtitle: Transform
items.contents:
Transform Component

Transform controls the Node's position, scale, and rotation.

PropertyMeaning
Position X/YWhere the Node is placed.
Scale X/YHow large the Node is horizontally and vertically.
AngleNode rotation.

items.subtitle: Text
items.contents:
Text Component

Text displays text in the game.

PropertyMeaning
TextThe text that is displayed.
Position X/YText position relative to the Node.
Font SizeText size.
Font FamilyFont used for the text.
FG ColorText color.
BG ColorBackground color.
BorderTurns the text border on or off.
Border ColorBorder color.
Border WidthBorder thickness.
Corner RadiusRounds the border/background corners.

items.subtitle: Sprite
items.contents:
Sprite Component

Sprite displays an image from your Asset Manager.

PropertyWhat you can do
TypeChoose between a normal Sprite and an Animation presentation.
SpriteChoose the image asset to display.
AnimationChoose an animation when the Sprite is using an animation source.
PixelatedKeep hard pixel edges for pixel-art style images.
Position X/YMove the image relative to the Node's Transform.
Size X/YSet the Sprite's local size relative to the Node Transform.

Because Sprite Position and Size are local to the Node, moving, scaling, or rotating the Node also affects the Sprite. This lets one Node act as the parent transform for its visual.

You can also click a Sprite in the Asset Manager to create a new Node that already has a Sprite component pointing to that exact asset. The Asset Manager closes after the Node is created so you can immediately continue editing the new Node.

items.subtitle: Animation Sprite
items.contents:
Animation Sprite Component

Animation Sprite stores animations made from Sprite frames.

PropertyMeaning
Animation NameName of an animation.
FPSHow many frames play each second.
FramesSprite images used by the animation.
Active AnimationThe animation currently selected for use.

items.subtitle: Physics
items.contents:
Physics Component

Physics gives a Node physical movement and collision behavior.

PropertyMeaning
BodyStatic, Kinematic, or Dynamic.
GravityGravity applied to Dynamic bodies.
FrictionResistance during contact.
BouncinessHow much an object rebounds.
Fixed RotationPrevents physics from rotating the body.
isColliderAllows the physics body to participate as a physical collider.

items.subtitle: Collider
items.contents:
Collider Component

Collider defines a collision shape independently from the Node's main Transform.

PropertyMeaning
ColliderTurns the collider on or off.
TypeRect, Circle, or Triangle.
Position X/YLocal collider offset relative to the Node.
Scale X/YLocal collider size/scale.
AngleLocal collider rotation.

items.subtitle: Progress Bar
items.contents:
Progress Bar Component

Progress Bar displays a value using a background and a filled area.

PropertyMeaning
Width / HeightBar size.
ValueCurrent value.
Min / MaxValue range.
Position X/YLocal position.
BG ColorBackground color.
Fill ColorFilled area color.
TL/TR/BR/BLCorner radii.
Outline Color / SizeOutline appearance.
DirectionFill direction.

items.subtitle: Joystick
items.contents:
Joystick Component

Joystick is a screen control for touch input.

PropertyMeaning
VariableName used to identify the joystick.
BG ColorJoystick base color.
Knob ColorJoystick knob color.
SizeJoystick width and height.
Left / Top / Right / BottomPositioning offsets from the screen edges.

Joystick input can be used by the onJoystick event and the Expression Library.

items.subtitle: Required Components
items.contents:
Required Components

Every Node includes Node, Script, and Transform. These stay available on the Node and are not removed like optional visual or gameplay Components.

items.subtitle: What is a variable?
items.contents:
Variables

A variable stores a value that your game can read or change. Variables are useful for scores, health, names, counters, states, settings, and switches.

items.subtitle: Global Variables
items.contents:
Global Variables

Global variables belong to the whole project. They can be used across Scenes.

Example expression: ctx.global.score.

items.subtitle: Scene Variables
items.contents:
Scene Variables

Scene variables belong to one Scene. Each Scene can have its own values.

Example expression: ctx.sceneVariables.level.

items.subtitle: Local Variables
items.contents:
Local Variables

Local variables belong to one Node and its Script. Two different Nodes can have Local variables with the same name because they have separate local scopes.

Example expression: ctx.local.speed.

items.subtitle: Variable types
items.contents:
Variable types

Depending on where a value is used, you can work with text, numbers, true/false values, colors, selectors, or empty values.

items.subtitle: Variable name errors
items.contents:
Variable name errors

When a variable name is not allowed because it conflicts with another name, the editor rejects the change and shows a red error outline. The previous valid name is kept.

items.subtitle: onLoad
items.contents:
onLoad

Starts when the Node enters the active game Scene.

Inputs: none. Output: out.

Use it for setup that should happen when a Node starts.

items.subtitle: onTick
items.contents:
onTick

Runs repeatedly while the game is running.

Inputs: none. Output: out.

Useful for repeated checks and continuous behavior.

items.subtitle: onKeybind
items.contents:
onKeybind

Starts when a selected keyboard key or keybind is pressed.

Input: Keybind. Output: out.

items.subtitle: onTouch
items.contents:
onTouch

Responds to touch input.

Input: Event = up, down, or move. Output: out.

items.subtitle: onMouse
items.contents:
onMouse

Responds to mouse or pointer input.

Input: Event = up, down, or move. Output: out.

items.subtitle: onScreenInput
items.contents:
onScreenInput

Responds to pointer input using screen-space coordinates.

Input: Event = up, down, or move. Output: out.

items.subtitle: onJoystick
items.contents:
onJoystick

Responds to a selected Joystick control.

Input: Variable = the joystick name. Output: out.

items.subtitle: onUnload
items.contents:
onUnload

Starts when a Node leaves the active runtime Scene.

Inputs: none. Output: out.

items.subtitle: onConnectionChange
items.contents:
onConnectionChange

Runs when the device's network state changes between online and offline.

Input: Connection. Choose Online or Offline.

Output: out.

This is useful for games that need to change behavior when connectivity is lost or restored—for example, showing an offline message, pausing online-only actions, or starting a locally available fallback.

items.subtitle: onAudioPickup
items.contents:
onAudioPickup

Runs when the microphone audio level is detected as a pickup event while microphone use is enabled.

Output: out.

Read the current microphone loudness with ctx.mic.decibel. A simple use is to react when someone claps, speaks loudly, or creates another sound above the pickup threshold.

Microphone use must first be enabled in Game Settings. The browser may also ask the user for microphone permission.

items.subtitle: loadScene
items.contents:
loadScene

Changes to another Scene.

Input: Scene. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setVariable
items.contents:
setVariable

Changes a variable.

Inputs: Type (Global, Local, or Scene), Name, Value. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setTransform
items.contents:
setTransform

Changes the current Node's Transform.

Inputs: PosX, PosY, ScaleX, ScaleY, Angle. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setNode
items.contents:
setNode

Changes supported Node identity values during runtime.

Inputs: Name, Id. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setText
items.contents:
setText

Changes a Text component during runtime.

Inputs include Text, Position X/Y, Font Size, Font Family, foreground/background colors, and border settings. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setSprite
items.contents:
setSprite

Changes the visible Sprite or Animation selection.

Inputs: Type (Sprite or Animation), Sprite, Animation, Pixelated. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setPhysics
items.contents:
setPhysics

Changes the runtime Physics settings.

Inputs: Body, Gravity, Friction, Bounciness, Fixed Rotation, and collider participation. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setCollider
items.contents:
setCollider

Changes the runtime Collider.

Inputs: Collider enabled, Type (Rect/Circle/Triangle), Position X/Y, Scale X/Y, and Angle. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setProgressBar
items.contents:
setProgressBar

Changes a Progress Bar during runtime.

Inputs include Width, Height, Value, Min, Max, Position, colors, corner radii, outline, and direction. Output: out.

items.subtitle: Follow Object
items.contents:
Follow Object

Makes the current runtime object move directly toward a selected target using Physics velocity.

Inputs: Target and Speed. The current Node needs a Physics component. Without Physics, it does not move. The Node faces its movement direction unless Fixed Rotation is enabled.

References: Physics · Transform · setVelocity

items.subtitle: Destroy Object
items.contents:
Destroy Object

Removes the current runtime object from the game.

Inputs: none. Output: out.

items.subtitle: Create Object
items.contents:
Create Object

Creates a runtime copy of a selected Node.

Inputs: Object, PosX, PosY, Angle, VelocityX, VelocityY, AngularVelocity. Angle sets the new object’s starting rotation in degrees.

References: Transform · Physics · setVelocity

items.subtitle: setVelocity
items.contents:
setVelocity

Changes movement speed during runtime.

Inputs: VelocityX, VelocityY, AngularVelocity. Output: out.

items.subtitle: setCamera
items.contents:
setCamera

Changes the Scene Camera during runtime.

Inputs include Enabled, Follow, Position X/Y, Angle, Horizontal/Vertical movement, Animation, Speed, Scale, and Background Color. Output: out.

items.subtitle: playAudio
items.contents:
playAudio

Plays an Audio or MIDI asset at runtime.

InputWhat it controls
srcThe Audio or MIDI asset to play.
startStarting position in milliseconds. Use 0 to start at the beginning.
durationHow long to play in milliseconds. Use 0 to play until the source finishes.
loopRepeat playback while enabled.
fadeinFade in over the selected time.
fadeoutFade out over the selected time.

Example: start = 5000 begins around five seconds into the source, while duration = 1000 plays for one second.

items.subtitle: stopAudio
items.contents:
stopAudio

Stops active runtime audio.

Inputs: none. Output: out.

items.subtitle: clearAudio
items.contents:
clearAudio

Stops active runtime audio and clears the current runtime audio playback list.

Inputs: none. Output: out.

items.subtitle: startSpeechRecognition
items.contents:
startSpeechRecognition

Starts browser speech recognition when microphone use is enabled and the browser supports speech recognition.

You can use it when you want spoken words to become text during gameplay.

The current recognized text is available through ctx.mic.speech while recognition is running.

items.subtitle: stopSpeechRecognition
items.contents:
stopSpeechRecognition

Stops active speech recognition.

Use it when you no longer need speech input, such as when leaving a voice-controlled menu or ending a voice command.

items.subtitle: Chase
items.contents:
Chase

Chases a target while avoiding Collider Nodes inside the selected Map folder and its nested folders.

Inputs: Map, Target, Speed. Requires a Physics component on the current Node. It uses a lightweight pursuit plus local obstacle steering rather than a full navigation rebuild every frame.

The Node faces movement direction unless Fixed Rotation is enabled.

References: Folders · Collider · Physics · Follow Object

items.subtitle: Avoid
items.contents:
Avoid

Moves away from a target while avoiding Collider Nodes inside the selected Map folder and its nested folders.

Inputs: Map, Target, Speed. Requires a Physics component on the current Node. It uses the same obstacle steering as Chase, but reverses the target-seeking direction.

The Node faces movement direction unless Fixed Rotation is enabled.

References: Folders · Collider · Physics · Chase

items.subtitle: Boolean
items.contents:
Boolean

Checks a true/false value and gives separate outputs for the true and false paths.

Input: Value. Outputs: next, truth, falsy.

items.subtitle: Interval
items.contents:
Interval

Repeats a flow after the selected time interval.

Input: Milliseconds. Outputs: next and out. Default: 1000 ms. Both outputs fire when the interval occurs.

items.subtitle: Timeout
items.contents:
Timeout

Delays a flow once before continuing.

Input: Milliseconds. Outputs: next and out. Default: 1000 ms. Both outputs fire when the timeout completes.

items.subtitle: isCollidedWith
items.contents:
isCollidedWith

Checks whether the current Node is colliding with a selected target.

Input: Target. Outputs: next, truth, and falsy. next continues the flow whether the collision result is true or false.

items.subtitle: What is an expression?
items.contents:
Expressions

An expression lets an input use a calculated value instead of a fixed value. You can type expressions or choose helpers from the Expression Library.

items.subtitle: Variables in expressions
items.contents:
Variables in expressions

Use the matching variable scope when reading a variable.

ctx.global.score
ctx.sceneVariables.level
ctx.local.speed

items.subtitle: Input and event values
items.contents:
Input and event values

Expressions can use keyboard, touch, mouse, screen-input, and joystick values provided by the current game state.

items.subtitle: Transform and velocity values
items.contents:
Transform and velocity values

Expressions can read position, scale, angle, and velocity values for the current Node.

ctx.position.x
ctx.position.y
ctx.scale.x
ctx.scale.y
ctx.angle
ctx.velocity.velocityX
ctx.velocity.velocityY
ctx.velocity.angularVelocity

items.subtitle: Math functions
items.contents:
Math functions

FunctionArgumentsUse
Math.lerp(a, b, t)Interpolate between two values.
Math.clamp(value, min, max)Keep a value inside a range.
Math.map(value, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax)Convert one range to another.
Math.moveTowards(current, target, maxDelta)Move toward a target.
Math.smoothstep(a, b, t)Smoothly interpolate.
Math.wrap(value, min, max)Wrap a value into a range.
Math.degToRad(degrees)Convert degrees to radians.
Math.radToDeg(radians)Convert radians to degrees.
Math.distance(a, b)Distance between two 2D vectors.
Math.randInt(min, max)Random whole number from min through max.

items.subtitle: Common JavaScript math
items.contents:
Common Math functions

You can also use standard JavaScript Math functions supported by the expression field, such as Math.abs, Math.floor, Math.ceil, Math.round, Math.sqrt, Math.pow, Math.sin, Math.cos, Math.tan, Math.atan2, Math.min, and Math.max.

items.subtitle: Vectors
items.contents:
Vectors

FunctionArgumentsUse
vec2(x, y)Create a 2D vector.
length(v)Get vector length.
dot(a, b)Get the dot product.
normalize(v)Turn a vector into a unit direction.

items.subtitle: Function argument hints
items.contents:
Function argument hints

The Expression Library shows function names together with their argument names, such as Math.randInt(min, max), so you can see what values the function expects before using it.

items.subtitle: Microphone expressions
items.contents:
Microphone expressions

When microphone use is enabled and permission is available, the Expression Library provides a Mic group.

ExpressionMeaning
ctx.mic.decibelCurrent microphone loudness level.
ctx.mic.speechCurrent speech-recognition text while recognition is active.
ctx.mic.activeWhether microphone input is currently active.
ctx.mic.speechActiveWhether speech recognition is currently running.

These values are intended for runtime expressions, such as showing a live microphone meter, reacting to a sound level, or displaying recognized speech.

items.subtitle: JavaScript values and operators
items.contents:
JavaScript values and operators

Expression fields use JavaScript-style expressions for calculations and conditions. The basic pieces you will use most often are numbers, strings, booleans, properties, arithmetic, comparisons, and logical operators.

SyntaxExampleMeaning
Arithmetic10 + 5 * 2Calculate numbers.
Comparisonctx.global.score >= 100Check a condition.
Equalityctx.local.state === "dead"Check whether two values are equal.
Not equalctx.local.health !== 0Check whether values differ.
ANDa && bBoth conditions must be true.
ORa || bAt least one condition must be true.
NOT!ctx.local.deadReverse a boolean value.

items.subtitle: Ternary operator
items.contents:
Ternary operator

The ternary operator chooses one of two values using a condition:

condition ? truth : falsy

For example:

ctx.global.score >= 100 ? "Winner" : "Keep Playing"

If the condition is true, the expression produces "Winner". Otherwise it produces "Keep Playing".

This is useful when an input needs one value for one case and another value for the opposite case.

items.subtitle: Optional chaining
items.contents:
Optional chaining ?.

Optional chaining lets you safely read a property when an earlier value might not exist.

ctx.node?.name

Without optional chaining, trying to read a property from a missing value can cause an error. With ?., the result becomes undefined instead of stopping the expression at that point.

It can also be used through a chain:

ctx.node?.sprite?.src

Use it when an object or Component may be absent.

items.subtitle: Nullish coalescing
items.contents:
Nullish coalescing ??

?? supplies a fallback when the value on its left is null or undefined.

ctx.local.name ?? "Player"

If ctx.local.name has a real value, that value is used. If it is missing, "Player" is used instead.

This is different from using || when you need to keep valid values such as 0 or false.

items.subtitle: Property and bracket access
items.contents:
Property and bracket access

Use a dot to read a normal property:

ctx.position.x
ctx.global.score

Use brackets when the property name is dynamic or is not a convenient identifier:

ctx.events.key["1"]
ctx.local["player-name"]

Bracket access is also useful when a value comes from another expression.

items.subtitle: Parentheses and order
items.contents:
Parentheses and order

Parentheses let you make the intended order of a calculation explicit.

(ctx.global.score + 10) * 2

Without parentheses, multiplication is evaluated before addition. Use parentheses whenever a long expression could be confusing or when a comparison is combined with several logical operators.

items.subtitle: Scene Camera
items.contents:
Scene Camera

The Scene Camera controls what part of the game world the player sees.

Common settings include Enabled, Follow, Position, Horizontal and Vertical movement, Animation, Speed, Scale, Angle, and Background Color.

items.subtitle: Camera Follow
items.contents:
Camera Follow

The camera can follow This or another Node selected from the Scene.

items.subtitle: Camera Animation
items.contents:
Camera Animation

Quick changes the camera immediately. Smooth moves toward the target over time using the camera speed.

items.subtitle: Camera Scale
items.contents:
Camera Scale

Camera scale changes how close or wide the world appears through the camera.

items.subtitle: Screen Type
items.contents:
Screen Type

Game Settings controls how the game's logical view fits the physical screen.

The available modes are Windowboxing, Stretch, Crop, and Smart Camera.

items.subtitle: Windowboxing
items.contents:
Windowboxing

Windowboxing is the default screen type. The 16:9 game view keeps its shape and unused space appears as black bars.

items.subtitle: Stretch
items.contents:
Stretch

Stretch fills the physical screen. The game view can look wider or taller when the screen is not the same shape as the game view.

items.subtitle: Crop
items.contents:
Crop

Crop fills the screen while keeping the game view shape, but parts of the world may be cut off at the edges.

items.subtitle: Smart Camera
items.contents:
Smart Camera

Smart Camera changes the visible camera area to match the physical screen shape instead of stretching the image.

items.subtitle: Required Features
items.contents:
Required features

Some ScriptNodes can depend on a feature that your game must explicitly enable. A Node can still show those ScriptNodes in the library, but the ScriptNode is disabled until its requirement is enabled.

When you click a disabled required ScriptNode, the editor can offer to take you to Game Settings so you can enable the required feature.

items.subtitle: Use Mic
items.contents:
Use Mic

Use Mic enables microphone features for the game.

When enabled, the runtime requests microphone permission from the browser the first time the running game needs the microphone. If permission was already granted, the game can continue without asking again.

Microphone-powered features include ctx.mic.decibel, onAudioPickup, and speech recognition actions.

Turning the setting off prevents microphone-dependent features from being usable.

items.subtitle: Speech recognition settings
items.contents:
Speech recognition settings

When Use Mic is enabled, you can choose the Speech Language and whether speech recognition is Continuous and uses Live Interim Results.

items.subtitle: What is the Asset Manager?
items.contents:
Asset Manager

The Asset Manager is where you keep the image, audio, and MIDI files used by your project.

items.subtitle: Supported asset types
items.contents:
Asset types

TypeExamples
Image/SpritePNG, JPEG, SVG and supported image files.
AudioMP3, WAV, OGG, M4A and other supported audio files.
MIDIMID and MIDI files.

items.subtitle: Importing assets
items.contents:
Importing assets

You can use the Import button or drag and drop a file into the asset area.

Only supported image and audio files are accepted by the drag-and-drop area. Unsupported file types are rejected instead of being added as assets.

items.subtitle: Drag and Drop
items.contents:
Drag and Drop

The asset area shows a drop target next to the Import control. Drag a supported image or audio file onto it to import the file.

items.subtitle: Asset names
items.contents:
Asset names

Imported files receive project asset names. When a name is already in use, the editor chooses another available name instead of silently replacing the existing asset.

items.subtitle: Rename Audio
items.contents:
Rename Audio

In the Audio section, press the ✎ Edit button for an audio asset. The editor asks for a new name. Enter the name you want to use and confirm it to rename the asset.

items.subtitle: Using assets
items.contents:
Using assets

Sprite assets are used by Sprite and Animation Sprite Components. Audio and MIDI assets are used by audio playback and related ScriptNodes.

items.subtitle: Clicking a Sprite
items.contents:
Clicking a Sprite

Clicking a Sprite in the Asset Manager creates a new Node using the same Node-creation path as + Add Node.

The new Node includes a Sprite Component and its Sprite source is already set to the clicked Sprite asset. You can then edit the Node normally.

items.subtitle: Sprite selection
items.contents:
Sprite selection

Sprite selection uses the same card-style image layout as the Asset Manager, keeping each image inside its own preview area without overlapping other images.

items.subtitle: Click a Sprite to create a Node
items.contents:
Click a Sprite to create a Node

Clicking a Sprite in the Asset Manager creates a new Node using the same normal Node creation path as + Add Node. The new Node receives a Sprite Component whose source points to the selected Sprite asset.

The Asset Manager closes automatically after the Node is created.

items.subtitle: Sprite asset shortcut
items.contents:
Sprite asset shortcut

Clicking an image in the Sprites section can immediately create a new Node using that image.

  1. Open the Asset Manager.
  2. Click the Sprite image you want.
  3. Node2D creates a Node using the same Node-creation path as + Add Node.
  4. A Sprite Component is added to that Node.
  5. The Sprite's source is set to the exact asset you clicked.
  6. The Asset Manager closes automatically.

This is useful when you want to place an imported image in the Scene without manually creating a Node and then searching for the same asset again.

items.subtitle: Audio preview
items.contents:
Audio preview

Clicking an Audio asset opens a preview modal before you use it in a ScriptNode. Use the preview controls to test whether you imported the expected sound.

This lets you check a sound directly from the Asset Manager instead of repeatedly starting the game just to hear the asset.

items.subtitle: Sprite Editor overview
items.contents:
Sprite Editor

The Sprite Editor is used for pixel-based image editing and Sprite frames.

items.subtitle: Drawing tools
items.contents:
Drawing tools

Common tools include Pencil, Eraser, Line, Rectangle, Ellipse, Triangle, Fill, and color picking.

items.subtitle: Selections
items.contents:
Selections

Box and lasso selections let you isolate part of a Sprite. You can move, copy, cut, delete, flip, mirror, rotate, and transform the selected pixels where supported.

items.subtitle: Multiple frames
items.contents:
Frames

Sprites can have multiple frames. Frames can be added, copied, reordered, removed, and previewed as an animation.

items.subtitle: Zoom and grid
items.contents:
Zoom and grid

Use zoom and grid controls for pixel-level work. The editing view can be enlarged for precise drawing.

items.subtitle: MIDI Editor overview
items.contents:
MIDI Editor

The MIDI Editor is a piano-roll editor for creating and editing MIDI music. You can draw, erase, move, resize, select, copy, paste, duplicate, and delete notes.

items.subtitle: MIDI name
items.contents:
Changing the MIDI name

The MIDI name is shown beside MIDI Editor. Double-click the name to edit it directly. Press Enter or click elsewhere to save the new name.

items.subtitle: Cancel
items.contents:
Cancel

Canceling the MIDI Editor asks for confirmation before leaving, so you have a chance to avoid losing the current editing session.

items.subtitle: Tracks
items.contents:
Tracks

A MIDI file can contain multiple tracks. Select a track to edit its notes and use the track controls to add or remove tracks where available.

items.subtitle: Notes
items.contents:
Notes

A note has a pitch, time position, duration, and velocity. Notes can be drawn, moved, resized, copied, duplicated, and deleted.

items.subtitle: Note selection
items.contents:
Note selection

Use click selection and marquee selection to select multiple notes. Ctrl/Cmd-click can add or remove individual notes, and Shift can select ranges where supported.

items.subtitle: Snap and length
items.contents:
Snap and length

Snap sets the timing grid used for note placement and movement. Length controls the note timing length used by the editor.

items.subtitle: BPM
items.contents:
BPM

BPM controls playback tempo.

items.subtitle: Playback and loop
items.contents:
Playback and loop

Use Play, Stop, Rewind, and Loop to preview the MIDI while editing.

items.subtitle: MIDI loading progress
items.contents:
MIDI loading progress

When a MIDI file is being edited or loaded, the editor shows a loading progress bar with a percentage. This makes it clear that a large MIDI file is still being processed.

items.subtitle: Import and Export
items.contents:
Import and Export

Import loads a MIDI file into the editor. Export writes the edited MIDI sequence back to a MIDI file.

items.subtitle: Changing the MIDI name
items.contents:
Changing the MIDI name

The MIDI name is shown beside MIDI Editor.

  1. Double-click the name.
  2. The normal text becomes directly editable.
  3. Type the new name.
  4. Press Enter or click somewhere else to apply it.

The rename changes the project asset name rather than changing the musical notes.

items.subtitle: Cancel editing
items.contents:
Cancel editing

Cancel asks for confirmation before leaving the MIDI Editor. This gives you a chance to stop the cancellation if you changed your mind and want to keep editing.

items.subtitle: Playing audio
items.contents:
Playing audio

Use the audio controls or the playAudio ScriptNode to play an Audio or MIDI asset during runtime.

items.subtitle: Audio options
items.contents:
Audio options

Playback can use duration, looping, fade-in, and fade-out settings where supported by the selected playback control.

items.subtitle: Stopping audio
items.contents:
Stopping audio

Use the available stop control or the stopAudio ScriptNode to stop active playback.

items.subtitle: Audio preview
items.contents:
Audio preview

Click an Audio asset in the Audio section to open an Audio Preview modal. Use the audio controls there to play and test the sound before using it with playAudio.

The preview does not change the asset or create a game object.

items.subtitle: New Project
items.contents:
New Project

Creates a fresh project with the normal starting project settings and a starting Scene.

items.subtitle: Save Project
items.contents:
Save Project

Save stores your current project so it can be reopened later.

items.subtitle: Load Project
items.contents:
Load Project

Load opens a previously saved local project.

items.subtitle: Import NDC
items.contents:
Import NDC

Import NDC loads a complete project file containing your Scenes, Nodes, Components, Scripts, settings, and project assets.

items.subtitle: Export NDC
items.contents:
Export NDC

Export NDC saves the complete project as one portable project file.

items.subtitle: Export Project
items.contents:
Export Project

Export Project creates a playable web package containing the project and the runtime files needed to run it.

items.subtitle: Current project on reload
items.contents:
Current project on reload

Node2D remembers which local project is currently loaded during the browser session. When you reload the page, the editor can automatically reopen that project instead of dropping you back at the project chooser.

This is especially useful when refreshing the page during development. Closing the tab or ending the browser session clears session-only information according to normal browser session storage behavior.

items.subtitle: Play
items.contents:
Play

Play starts the Preferred Scene using the project settings, scripts, input, camera, physics, audio, and variables.

items.subtitle: Debug
items.contents:
Debug

Debug runs the game while exposing additional information intended to help you inspect what is happening during runtime.

items.subtitle: Runtime changes
items.contents:
Runtime changes

Changes made while the game is running affect the running game state. They are separate from changing the saved project in the editor.

items.subtitle: Scene changes during runtime
items.contents:
Scene changes

A ScriptNode can change the current runtime Scene using loadScene.

items.subtitle: Editor Settings
items.contents:
Editor Settings

Editor Settings contains preferences for the editor, including editable keyboard shortcuts.

items.subtitle: Shortcut preference storage
items.contents:
Shortcut preferences

Your chosen editor shortcuts are saved locally on your device, so the editor can reuse them after you close and reopen it.

items.subtitle: Download Preferences
items.contents:
Download Preferences

Download Pref... saves your editor preferences as JSON.

The export includes the stored editor preference data rather than only a manually selected list. This allows preferences introduced by a future editor version to travel with the downloaded settings when they are stored in the preference data.

Your chosen keyboard shortcuts, Move / Scale Snap, Rotate Snap, Auto Save, and Auto Save Interval are included when they are stored as editor preferences.

items.subtitle: Move / Scale Snap
items.contents:
Move / Scale Snap

Sets the fixed editing interval used by Node movement and scaling.

Default: 1.

Examples:

  • 1 → values move/scale in whole-unit steps.
  • 0.5 → values use half-unit steps.
  • 0.1 → values use one-tenth-unit steps.
  • 0 → no movement/scale snapping.

The setting is saved with your editor preferences.

items.subtitle: Rotate Snap
items.contents:
Rotate Snap

Sets the fixed angle interval used by the Rotate gizmo.

0° (Off) allows free rotation. A value such as 90° makes the rotation land on right-angle increments.

Rotation snapping is independent from Move / Scale Snap.

items.subtitle: Auto Save
items.contents:
Auto Save

Enable Auto Save when you want Node2D to periodically save the currently loaded project instead of relying only on manual saves.

Auto Save applies to the loaded project. It does not replace exporting a project when you need a portable file.

items.subtitle: Auto Save Interval
items.contents:
Auto Save Interval

This controls how often Auto Save runs, in seconds.

For example, 30 s means the current project is automatically saved about every 30 seconds while Auto Save is enabled.

Set a shorter interval when you are doing frequent small edits. Use a longer interval when you are making large groups of changes.

items.subtitle: Prevent accidental reload or close
items.contents:
Prevent accidental reload or close

When a project is loaded, the editor prevents common accidental reload shortcuts such as F5 and Ctrl/Cmd+R and asks the browser for confirmation when the page is being reloaded or closed.

items.subtitle: Reset Defaults
items.contents:
Reset Defaults

Reset Defaults restores the editor settings to their default values and restores the default keyboard shortcuts. The current editor preference values are replaced by the defaults.

SettingDefault
Move / Scale Snap1
Rotate Snap0° (Off)
Auto SaveOff
Auto Save Interval30 Seconds

items.subtitle: Import Preferences
items.contents:
Import Preferences

Import Pref... loads an editor preference JSON file previously downloaded from Node2D. Stored editor settings and saved shortcut choices are restored from the file, so the editor changes to match the imported preferences.

The import can also restore stored preference keys contained in the exported preference data, allowing newer preference values to be carried between editor versions.

items.subtitle: Project shortcuts
items.contents:
Project shortcuts

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+SSave
Ctrl+NNew Project
Ctrl+OOpen / Load
Ctrl+EExport

items.subtitle: Editing shortcuts
items.contents:
Editing shortcuts

ShortcutAction
Ctrl+CCopy
Ctrl+XCut
Ctrl+VPaste
Ctrl+DDuplicate
Delete / BackspaceDelete
F2Rename
Ctrl+ASelect All
Ctrl+Shift+ADeselect All
Ctrl+ZUndo
Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+ZRedo

items.subtitle: View and runtime shortcuts
items.contents:
View and runtime

ShortcutAction
SpacePlay / Stop
F11Fullscreen
Ctrl+=Zoom In
Ctrl+-Zoom Out
Ctrl+0Reset Zoom

EscapeClose / Cancel

items.subtitle: Node tool shortcuts
items.contents:
Node tool shortcuts

KeyTool
1Select
2Move
3Rotate
4Scale
5All

These shortcuts can be changed in Editor Settings.

items.subtitle: Automatic offline mode
items.contents:
Automatic offline mode

Node2D can maintain a saved browser copy of the editor for offline use.

  1. Online: the editor loads the current files and updates the saved offline copy.
  2. Offline: the browser loads the saved copy when the network is unavailable.
  3. Back online: the editor can request the newest files again so your offline copy can catch up.

This caching is browser storage for web resources; it is not a normal file download into your Downloads folder.

items.subtitle: Offline toast
items.contents:
Offline message

When the editor starts using its saved offline copy, it shows a notification so you know that Offline Mode is active.

items.subtitle: PWA installation
items.contents:
PWA

The editor itself can be used as a Progressive Web App when the browser supports installation. This is separate from exporting a game as a PWA: the editor can also have its own installable/offline behavior.

items.subtitle: Landscape PWA preference
items.contents:
Landscape PWA preference

The Node2D Game Engine PWA manifest requests landscape orientation. On browsers and installed-app environments that support the manifest orientation setting, the installed app prefers to open in landscape.

items.subtitle: A variable name was rejected
items.contents:
Variable name rejected

Choose a name that is not already used in a conflicting scope. The editor keeps the last valid name and shows the field with red error styling when a conflict is detected.

items.subtitle: An asset was rejected
items.contents:
Asset rejected

Check that the file is a supported image or audio type for the drop/import area you are using. Unsupported file types are intentionally rejected.

items.subtitle: The game view does not fit the screen
items.contents:
Game view fitting

Check Game Settings → Screen Type. Windowboxing keeps the 16:9 shape, Stretch fills the screen, Crop fills the screen while cutting edges, and Smart Camera changes the visible camera area.

items.subtitle: A MIDI file is still loading
items.contents:
MIDI loading

Large MIDI files can take time to process. Watch the loading percentage shown by the MIDI Editor instead of assuming the editor is frozen.

items.subtitle: The editor is too narrow
items.contents:
Editor too narrow

Rotate the device or expand the window when the editor displays the small-screen warning. Editing is intentionally blocked while the screen is too narrow.

items.subtitle: Objects move by tiny decimal amounts
items.contents:
Objects move by tiny decimal amounts

Check Editor Settings → Move / Scale Snap. A value such as 0.1 makes the position and scale use tenth-unit steps while the gizmo is dragged.

Snapping is applied to the Move gizmo center/axes and to the Scale gizmo handles. Rotation has its own separate snap setting.

items.subtitle: Scale corner does not keep the ratio
items.contents:
Scale corner behavior

Use a corner handle when you want a proportional resize. Corner handles preserve the starting width-to-height ratio. Use a side handle when you intentionally want to change only width or only height.

items.subtitle: ScriptNode placement
items.contents:
ScriptNode placement

When adding a ScriptNode from the library, Node2D places it at the center of the currently visible Script canvas, taking the current pan and zoom into account. Dragging a ScriptNode into the canvas places it at the actual drop location.

items.subtitle: Components
items.contents:
Components

Node — object identity. Script — visual script graph. Transform — position, scale, rotation. Text — displayed text. Sprite — images and animated presentation. Animation Sprite — collections of sprite frames. Physics — physical movement. Collider — collision shape. Progress Bar — value meter. Joystick — touch control.

items.subtitle: Events
items.contents:
Events

onLoad, onTick, onKeybind, onTouch, onMouse, onScreenInput, onJoystick, onAudioPickup, onConnectionChange, onUnload.

items.subtitle: Actions
items.contents:
Actions

loadScene, setVariable, setTransform, setNode, setText, setSprite, setPhysics, setCollider, setProgressBar, Follow Object, Chase, Avoid, Destroy Object, Create Object, setVelocity, setCamera, playAudio, startSpeechRecognition, stopSpeechRecognition, stopAudio, clearAudio.

items.subtitle: Controls
items.contents:
Controls

Boolean, Interval, Timeout, isCollidedWith. Control nodes provide a next flow where supported so execution can continue without needing a special timer or collision node.

items.subtitle: New Event: onConnectionChange
items.contents:
onConnectionChange

onConnectionChange is an Event ScriptNode with a Connection selector containing Online and Offline. It sends out when the browser changes network connection state while the game is running.

items.subtitle: Editor Snap
items.contents:
Editor Snap

Default Move / Scale Snap: 1. Default Rotate Snap: 0° (Off). Both settings can be changed in Editor Settings and are saved on your device.

items.subtitle: Audio playback inputs
items.contents:
Audio playback inputs

playAudio uses src, start, duration, loop, fadein, and fadeout. A duration of 0 means play until the asset finishes.

items.subtitle: New microphone ScriptNodes
items.contents:
Microphone ScriptNodes

Events: onAudioPickup. Actions: startSpeechRecognition and stopSpeechRecognition. These require Use Mic to be enabled in Game Settings.

items.subtitle: Requirements
items.contents:
ScriptNode requirements

A ScriptNode can require a Game Settings feature. Required ScriptNodes remain visible but are disabled until the required feature is enabled.

items.subtitle: Editor Settings defaults
items.contents:
Editor Settings defaults

Default editing snap is 1, Rotate Snap is 0° (Off), Auto Save is off, and Auto Save Interval is 30 Seconds. Use Reset Defaults to restore these values and the default shortcuts.

items.subtitle: Export Project
items.contents:
Export Project

Export Project creates a playable web package from the project you are editing. It is meant for sharing or hosting the game, not for continuing to edit the project.

The exported package contains a launcher page, the project data, and the runtime files needed to load the project. Your Scenes, Nodes, Components, ScriptNode graphs, variables, camera/game settings, and project assets are represented in the project data.

The export process reads the current engine files at export time, so a newly exported package uses the runtime build from the editor you exported from.

Typical use

  1. Save the project.
  2. Choose Export Project.
  3. Wait for the export progress to finish.
  4. Open the resulting web package from a web-capable location.
  5. Test the exported game separately from the editor.

Use NDC export when you want the editable project data. Use Project Export when you want a playable web build.

items.subtitle: PWA export and offline use
items.contents:
PWA export and offline use

A PWA-capable export includes the information a browser needs to treat the exported game as an installable web application when the browser and hosting environment support it.

Offline caching lets the browser keep a local copy of the web app so the exported game can continue to open without downloading the same files again while offline.

items.subtitle: Numbers and arithmetic
items.contents:
Numbers and arithmetic

Use normal arithmetic in expressions: + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide, and % get the remainder.

ctx.local.speed * 2
ctx.global.score + 10
ctx.velocity.velocityX / 60

items.subtitle: Comparisons
items.contents:
Comparisons

Comparisons produce true or false.

ctx.local.health > 0
ctx.global.score >= 100
ctx.local.state === "ready"
ctx.local.state !== "dead"

items.subtitle: Logical operators
items.contents:
Logical operators

&& means AND, || means OR, and ! means NOT.

ctx.local.health > 0 && ctx.global.score > 100
ctx.local.state === "win" || ctx.local.state === "draw"
!ctx.local.dead

items.subtitle: Ternary
items.contents:
Ternary

Choose between two values:

condition ? truth : falsy
ctx.local.health > 0 ? "Alive" : "Dead"

items.subtitle: Optional chaining
items.contents:
Optional chaining

?. safely reads through a value that might be missing.

ctx.node?.name
ctx.node?.sprite?.src

items.subtitle: Nullish fallback
items.contents:
Nullish fallback

?? uses the value on the left unless it is null or undefined.

ctx.local.name ?? "Player"

items.subtitle: Property access
items.contents:
Property access

Use . to access named properties.

ctx.position.x
ctx.scale.y
ctx.global.score

items.subtitle: Bracket access
items.contents:
Bracket access

Use brackets when a property name needs to be written as a string.

ctx.events.key["1"]
ctx.local["player-name"]

items.subtitle: Parentheses
items.contents:
Parentheses

Use parentheses to control the order of a calculation and make complex expressions easier to read.

(ctx.global.score + 10) * 2

items.subtitle: Combining syntax
items.contents:
Combining syntax

These pieces can be combined into one expression.

ctx.node?.name === "Player" && (ctx.global.score >= 100 ? true : false)

Build complex expressions from small understandable pieces and test them in the input where they will be used.

items.subtitle: New ScriptNode placement
items.contents:
New ScriptNode placement

When you add a ScriptNode from the ScriptNode Library, Node2D places it at the center of the ScriptNode canvas view. If you have already panned or zoomed the graph, the new ScriptNode is placed at the center of the area you are currently looking at rather than at a fixed screen corner.

Dragging a ScriptNode from the library onto the canvas is different: it is placed at the exact drop location.

items.subtitle: Follow Object
items.contents:
Follow Object

Makes the current Node move directly toward a selected target using the Node’s Physics velocity.

Inputs: Target and Speed. The current Node must have a Physics component. Without Physics, the behavior does nothing.

The movement direction is updated continuously. When the target is reached, the movement velocity is stopped. The Node faces the direction of movement unless Physics Fixed Rotation is enabled.

References: Physics · Transform · setVelocity

items.subtitle: Create Object
items.contents:
Create Object

Creates a runtime copy of a selected Node.

Inputs: Object, PosX, PosY, Angle, VelocityX, VelocityY, and AngularVelocity. The new Angle is the starting rotation in degrees.

References: Transform · Physics · setVelocity

items.subtitle: Chase
items.contents:
Chase

Makes the current Node pursue a target while using a selected folder as its obstacle map.

Inputs: Map, Target, and Speed. The Map selector chooses a Folder. Its child Nodes are searched recursively; Nodes with a Collider become obstacles.

Chase uses a lightweight pursuit direction based on the target’s current movement, then combines it with local obstacle avoidance. It samples a small set of nearby movement directions instead of running a full pathfinder every frame, which keeps the behavior suitable for real-time gameplay. This is a hybrid steering approach based on the common seek/pursuit/flee and obstacle-avoidance behaviors described by Craig Reynolds.

The current Node must have a Physics component. Without Physics, the behavior does nothing. The Node faces its movement direction unless Physics Fixed Rotation is enabled.

References: Folders · Collider · Physics · Follow Object

items.subtitle: Avoid
items.contents:
Avoid

Makes the current Node move away from a selected target while using a selected folder as its obstacle map.

Inputs: Map, Target, and Speed. The Map selector chooses a Folder. Its child Nodes are searched recursively; Nodes with a Collider become obstacles.

Avoid uses the same lightweight obstacle-steering pass as Chase, but reverses the target direction. In other words, Chase seeks the target while Avoid flees from it. Obstacle avoidance is kept separate from flee direction so walls are treated as obstacles rather than simply causing the Node to run away from the wall.

Reference: Craig Reynolds, “Steering Behaviors for Autonomous Characters” (1999).

The current Node must have a Physics component. Without Physics, the behavior does nothing. The Node faces its movement direction unless Physics Fixed Rotation is enabled.

References: Folders · Collider · Physics · Chase

items.subtitle: Sliding numeric inputs
items.contents:
Sliding numeric inputs

Numeric ScriptNode inputs can be adjusted by horizontal swiping. Swipe left to decrease the value and right to increase it.

The step is based on the current value. For example, 3.42 uses a step of 0.01, while 3.4 uses 0.1 and 3 uses 1. This works directly on numeric ScriptNode inputs without opening the expression editor.

items.subtitle: Script viewport position
items.contents:
Script viewport position

Node2D remembers the pan and zoom position separately for each Node’s Script editor. Close the Script editor, open another Node’s Script, then return to the first one to get the same Script graph view back.

items.subtitle: Sprite Inspector on small screens
items.contents:
Sprite Inspector

The Sprite Editor keeps the Sprite Inspector available on narrow screens. When the editor is wider than the device can comfortably show, the Sprite Editor can use horizontal scrolling rather than removing the Inspector.

The Inspector contains the Sprite name, width, height, frame list, frame actions, playback controls, and FPS.

items.subtitle: Hidden Selection and Components panels
items.contents:
Hidden panels

When the Selection or Components panel is hidden, it no longer occupies visible editor space. A small S or C button appears beside the remaining dock so you can restore the hidden panel.

The buttons only appear for panels that are currently hidden.

items.subtitle: Script panel collapse
items.contents:
Collapsing Script panels

The Script Editor has a Local Variables/ScriptNode Library panel on the left and a Script Inspector on the right. Each side can be collapsed with its arrow button.

When collapsed, the side becomes a narrow strip while its arrow remains available to expand it again. This gives the Script canvas more room without closing the Script Editor.

items.subtitle: Resizing Script panels
items.contents:
Resizing Script panels

Drag the thin handle at the edge of either Script side panel to change its width. This works like resizing the Selection and Components dock.

items.subtitle: Fullscreen editor surfaces
items.contents:
Fullscreen editor surfaces

Large editing surfaces such as the Script Editor, Sprite Editor, MIDI Editor, Help, and Expression Editor can cover the full viewport. They no longer leave the main topbar visible behind them.

items.subtitle: PWA fullscreen
items.contents:
PWA fullscreen

When Node2D is installed as a Progressive Web App, its manifest requests the browser's fullscreen display mode. Supported browsers can therefore launch the installed Node2D app without normal browser UI around the app.

A normal browser tab still cannot be forced into fullscreen without a user gesture; the fullscreen PWA setting applies when the app is installed/launched as a PWA.

items.subtitle: Script panel resizing and collapse
items.contents:
Script panel resizing and collapse

In the Script Editor, the Local Variables/ScriptNode Library panel on the left and Script Inspector panel on the right can each be resized with their edge handle.

Use the arrow in a panel header to collapse that panel. When collapsed, its content no longer occupies the main canvas area. Use the same arrow to restore it.

items.subtitle: Sprite Editor side panels
items.contents:
Sprite Editor side panels

The Sprite Editor keeps both the Tools panel and Sprite Inspector available. Each side panel can be resized with its edge handle and collapsed with its header arrow.

On a narrow screen, the editor can scroll horizontally so the Inspector remains reachable instead of simply removing it from the editor.
